items.note: The Udaipur Prasasti glorifies Bhoja with building several temples dedicated to Kedaresvara, Ramesvara(?), Kalanala and Rudra
Merutunga says Bhoja rebuilt the city of Dhara; a Hoysala grant from Belur (1117 A.D.) says Dhara was made prosperous by Bhoja; all his temples since destroyed
D.C. Ganguly doubts Bhoja's part in building the Somanatha temple in Kathiawar or Ramesvara in south India; similar temples elsewhere
The most famous of Bhoja's temples was at Dhara, dedicated to Sarasvati and styled Sarasvati-Sadana or Bharati Bhavana
Sarasvati temple at Dhara said to be 200 by 117 feet; later converted by Mahmud Shah Khilji into the Kamalmoli mosque in Hijri Samvat 861 (V.S. 1514, A.D. 1457)
Bhoja erected several pillars; an iron pillar at Dhara probably set up by his general Kulachandra to celebrate victory over the Chalukyas of Gujarat

Muhammadan rulers of Malwa in the 15th century destroyed the temples of Dhara and reused the material, as in the Lat Masjid and the Kamalamaula mosque, where black slabs carrying Sanskrit inscriptions were used in the floor and mihrab
Two Sanskrit grammatical inscriptions in Nagari characters on two pillars in the mosque near Maulana Kamaluddin's tomb at Dhar, popularly called Bhojaraja-ki-Nisal or Raja Bhoja's College
Image of Sarasvati recording its installation in the temple of Raja Bhoja in Samvat 1091 (A.D. 1035) is in the British Museum, facsimile in Rupam
Two pillars in the Dhar mosque carry the Sanskrit alphabet and the verbal terminations, with two Sanskrit verses naming two successors of Raja Bhoja

A memorial of Bhoja's victory over the Chalukyas of the Deccan and Gangeya Chedi was converted into the Lat Masjid; inscription shows Dilawar Khan Ghori converted it in Hijri Samvat 807 (V.S. 1462, A.D. 1405)
The Kaliasot river was turned by the greater dam into the Betwa valley to feed the Bhojapur lake; the old bend of the Kaliasot can still be seen from the bund
The vast watery plains of the Bhojapur lake cooled the atmosphere for miles and held the water so that the river Betwa was never in floods
refs: Imperial Gazetteer of India VIII, p. 121

items.note: Shah Hussain of Mandu, about 400 years after it was built, had the dam broken, coveting the fertile silt-covered lake bed for agriculture

V.A. Smith: the great Bhojapur lake, formed by massive embankments closing the outlet in a circle of hills, testified to the engineers' skill until the 15th century, when a Muhammedan king cut the dam
refs: V.A. Smith, Early History of India, p. 411

items.note: Bhoja said to have built a Siva temple in the court of Chitor and named the Siva statue Bhoja Svamideva, also called Tribhuvana-Narayanadeva
Bhoja raised the fortress Mandapadurga with a college, built ghats and temples at Ujjayini; old fortifications of Dhara attributed to him; a great builder

Bhoja transferred his kingdom from Ujjayini to Dhara and beautified it; Parijatamanjari says palaces and pleasure gardens, 84 cross-roads and a demarcated palace area; palace circuit not less than three and a half miles
H.C. Ray: little evidence corroborates the extensive building the Udaipur Prasasti ascribes to Bhoja; Buhler thinks it very probable he adorned his capital with monuments, few surviving

claim.value: Ray: building claims little corroborated; Buhler: very probable

items.note: Verse 18 of the Udaipur Prasasti alludes to Bhoja's extensive knowledge and gives him the title Kaviraja, king of poets
Ain-e-Akbari says Bhoja's court had 400 selected scholars; Dhara was then the centre of political, intellectual and cultural activity
From A.D. 940 to 1050 Malwa and mainland Gujarat formed one kingdom whose greatest cultural centre was Dhara
In the Udaipur-prasasti Bhoja is praised for his kind head and heart
Bhoja daily went to the pavilion of distribution and gave gold to petitioners at his gate, a habit that made wide holes in the treasury
After Bhoja's death in c. A.D. 1054 the second empire of Gurjaradesa began to break up
Udaipur Prasasti on Bhoja's death: when the devotee of Bharga (Siva) went to the mansion of gods, the earth was filled with darkness of his foe and his hereditary warriors became infirm
The Udaipur prasasti styles Bhoja the illustrious poet king: he achieved, he gave, he knew

When Munja met his end the Malwa empire had almost collapsed; Bhoja with Malwa alone as patrimony extended the Paramara dominion three times its former size, from Chamba and Thaneswer to the Krishna and Tungabhadra
Of all Paramara rulers of Malwa Bhoja alone put several rulers to submission; the sayings of Alberuni and the Udaipur Prasasti that he was the most powerful king are called a bare fact
Religious tolerance marked Bhoja's time; Bhoja himself an ardent follower of Saivism yet patronised exponents of other sects with grants and donations
